title: Mr. Woodcock
full_review:
A comedy about the unfinished business of childhood, "Mr. Woodcock" (New Line) often strays beyond the bounds of good taste. But the film also has its moments of inspiration, and a few genuine insights as well.

When best-selling, self-help writer John Farley (Seann William Scott) learns he has been awarded the highest honor his small Midwestern hometown can bestow, he's thrilled, seeing it as the ultimate affirmation of his work. Over the strident protests of his hard-edged publicist, Maggie (Amy Poehler), he clears his calendar to attend the town's annual "Cornival" and receive his prize, the locally coveted "Corn Cob Key."

Once there, John finds that his widowed mother, Beverly (Susan Sarandon), has a surprise in store for him. She informs him that she's been dating his old gym teacher from junior high school, Mr. Woodcock (Billy Bob Thornton).

This, it turns out, is John's worst nightmare come true. Never mind that he has written the best-seller "Letting Go: Getting Past Your Past." John himself has never been able either to let go of or get past his experiences in Mr. Woodcock's physical education class. Outrageously harsh and unrelentingly demanding, Mr. Woodcock accepted no excuses from his students. He insulted them constantly and wielded a basketball like a weapon. Nor have his methods changed.

Determined to put an end to the relationship, John enlists the help of old friend and classmate Nedderman (Ethan Suplee). They try everything they can think of to discredit Mr. Woodcock in Beverly's eyes. Maggie, meanwhile, keeps warning John that he's endangering his professional future by obsessing about his past.

Director Craig Gillespie's film is at times needlessly crass, but is sporadically entertaining. Thornton's performance is especially enjoyable, his face throughout looking stonier than one of the faces on Mount Rushmore.

Perhaps the film's most thought-provoking passages are those that defend Mr. Woodcock's approach to educating his students. His demand for excellence and refusal to settle for mediocrity, the script implies, may be valuable qualities in an educator.

The film contains a nongraphic premarital sexual encounter, one use of the f-word, much crude and crass language, and innuendo. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
